utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm Dr. — good to meet you. I can see you've booked in about your lower back after lifting something on the weekend, and that it's really limiting you. Before we talk about scans, I'd like to understand exactly what's happened. Can you tell me in your own words what happened on the weekend, and how it's been since?
reply: On Saturday I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden and felt a twinge, then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been three days now. The pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock, and it is worse when I bend or get out of a chair, though it feels a bit better lying still with a heat pack and gets worse by the evening. I have worked from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
Daniel, here's the honest picture on the MRI. Your story and my examination show a straightforward muscle/joint strain with no sign of a slipped disc pressing on a nerve and none of the danger signs we screen for. In that situation, national guidelines actually recommend AGAINST scanning, for three reasons:

1. It won't change what we do — the treatment is the same whatever the scan shows, because the treatment is time, movement and pain relief.
2. Scans of healthy 41-year-olds almost always show "wear and tear" changes that have nothing to do with the pain, and those findings often cause unnecessary worry and sometimes lead to treatments people don't need.
3. It keeps the scan in reserve for when it would actually matter.

If things aren't improving over the next few weeks, or you develop leg pain, numbness or weakness, then a scan becomes appropriate and I'll arrange it promptly.
reply: I was really hoping to get a scan just to know for sure what is going on in there, but I suppose if the treatment is the same either way, I can try to manage it with movement and better pain relief.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course
Paracetamol as the analgesic

utterance:
Now the important safety-netting — please listen to this part:

Come back to see me, or go to an emergency department if it's after hours, STRAIGHT AWAY if you get any of these:
- Pain, numbness or weakness spreading down your leg, or trouble walking
- Any problem with your bladder or bowels — trouble passing urine, or loss of control
- Numbness around your bottom or genitals
- Fever, feeling unwell, or a hot red area over the spine

Otherwise, I'd like to see you back here in about 2 weeks to check your progress. If at that point it's not clearly improving, we'll look at physiotherapy and, if needed, revisit the question of a scan — with a clear reason by then.

Do you have any questions about any of that?
reply: Honestly, I have been reading online about slipped discs and people needing surgery, so I just want to know how I can be sure I am not going to end up needing an operation.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be

utterance:
That's a very fair question, and a common worry.

Here's how we can be confident: a "slipped disc" only becomes a surgical problem when it presses hard on a nerve — and that produces a very specific pattern: pain shooting down the leg below the knee, numbness, and weakness. You've just had a thorough nerve examination and every single one of those checks was normal: full strength in both legs, normal reflexes, normal sensation, and the tests that stretch the nerves didn't reproduce any leg pain. So there is no sign of nerve compression today.

And even for people who DO get a disc pressing on a nerve, the great majority — around 8 or 9 out of 10 — improve without surgery over a few months, because the body reabsorbs the disc material. Surgery is reserved for a small minority with severe, persistent nerve problems or the emergency bladder symptoms I mentioned.

What you have — pain staying in the back and buttock, worse with certain movements, better with rest and heat, normal nerves — is the classic pattern of a simple strain, and these heal with time and movement. The best thing you can do to protect your back long-term is exactly what we've discussed: stay active now, build back to regular exercise, strengthen your core and legs, and lift with your legs rather than your back next time there's a pot plant to move.

If anything changed — leg symptoms appearing, for example — we'd reassess immediately, and a scan would be on the table. Does that put your mind at ease?
reply: That actually does make me feel a lot better about it, thanks for explaining it so clearly.

awards.label: Defensible diagnosis: Lumbar muscle strain

Something can't be excluded here: the can't-miss slot needs it. Can't miss here: Cauda equina syndrome, Spinal malignancy (metastases or myeloma), Spinal infection (discitis or epidural abscess), Vertebral fracture, Abdominal aortic aneurysm
